newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: PARLIAMENT OBSERVES A MINUTE'S SILENCE
The Federal House of Representatives has observed a minute's silence to mark the national Reconciliation Convention, which began today in Melbourne.

Opposition leader Kim Beazley said he and the Prime Minister attended the opening of the conference, where a minute's silence was held to reflect upon the problems faced by indigenous people over the years.
He suggested it might also be appropriate for the House of Representaives.
John Howard agreed to the suggestion and the Speaker Bob Halverson called on members to commemorate a most auspicious event in Australia's history.
OPPOSITION BILL TO FREEZE CAR TARIFFS
Shadow Industry Minister, Simon Crean, says his private members to freeze car tariffs at 15 per cent gives Parliament a choice of having the car industry grow, or go down the gurgler.
A draft Industry Commission report recommmended car tariffs be cut to five percent by the year 2004.
Mr Crean says his bill would keep car tariffs at 15 per cent until at least the end of 2004, continue an export facilitation scheme and provide for a comprehensive review of the industry.
He says the bill would see ten thousand new jobs and a two to three hundred per cent increase in car exports.
APOLOGY A START- SAYS DODSON
The Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation says the Prime Minister's personal apology for hurt and trauma caused to indigenous people, is a start towards reconciliation.

Mr Howard told delegates at the Australian Reconciliation Convention in Melbourne, he feels deep sorrow for Aboriginal and Torres Strait islander people, who've suffered injustices under the practices of past generations.
But Mr Howard was heckled when he told delegates, Australians of this generation should not accept blame for past actions.
The Chairman of the Reconciliation Council, Pat Dodson, says the Prime Minister has exposed the challenges ahead for his Government.

But Mr Dodson defended delegates who booed Mr Howard, saying it's the only way they can display their dissatisfaction with the way the Government is handling matters such as Wik and the stolen generation.
HILL SAYS ACF SHOULD GET ON BOARD HERITAGE FUND
Federal Environment Minister, Robert Hill, says the Australian Conservation Foundation should recognise the wide community support for the Natural Heritage Trust.
The Foundation is concerned the money being spent on improving the environment as part of Trust will be wasted because the Government is doing little to stop land clearing in Australia.
However Senator Hill says it's time for the ACF to stop criticising the billion-dollar environment fund, and get on board.
He says the program has had about seven-thousand applications for community support.
CALL FOR MINING UNION TO SUPPORT WIK DECISION
ACTU secretary Bill Kelty has called on the mining and energy super union, the CFMEU, to back the High Court's Wik decision on native title.
Mr Kelty was opening the union's biennial conference on the Gold Coast.
Mining companies have seen the High Court's MABO decision as a threat to their plans.
But Mr Kelty told 300 union delegates that Aborigines'connection with the land, dating back thousands of years, justified them retaining some rights to their land.
HELP FOR YOUNG TO FIND JOBS AND HOUSING
The Federal Government says more than eight thousand people will be helped with jobs, housing and other problems over the next year under a new program.

The Job Placement, Employment and Training Projects is designed to help the homeless and young people at risk, tackle issues which prevent them from getting accommodation, education, training or employment.
Employment Minister Amanda Vanstone says the 11-million dollar scheme will give people under 21, support and advice on issues such as self esteem, family mediation and drug abuse.
She says the projects offer young Australians a chance to work towards achieving what they want from their lives.
MAN REMANDED OVER SALVOS FIRE
A 32-year-old man has appeared in court charged with beginning a huge fire at the Salvation Army's Wollongong store over the weekend.
Kevin Gibbs of Wollongong was given bail at a court hearing yesterday, but was remanded in custody today.
Police Prosecutor, Alex Popov told the court it was hard to imagine a more dangerous person in the community that the accused.
Mr Popov said Mr Gibbs had alleged to Police that he was capable of committing further offences of a serious nature.
John Gallagher from Legal Aid believed it would be better if Mr Gibbs could spend a week at the St Vincent De Paul Dexotification Centre under specific bail conditions.
However Magistrate, Paul Johnson, said while the accused had not pleaded guilty to the charge, there was a likelhood he could be sentenced to a lengthy jail term.
Magistrate Johnson said the threat to commit further offences had to be taken into account and remanded him in custody for two weeks.
